title: Chapter 52: Lot 41, Part 1 of 5: Tibbs
html:
Tibbs came at the eighth bell on Sunday morning, in the snow, with the key.
Lyra heard him before she saw him. She was sitting on the floor of the side vault with the Ledger open on her knees, reading Corin his first page, because Corin had asked her to. He read Oren his page every morning now, and somebody had to read Corin his. That was the rule they had made on Wednesday, in the crypt, when Silas told them about the knee. Somebody reads you your first page every morning, Vane, before you do anything. Somebody who isn't you. So it was Lyra. It had been Lyra every morning since.
She was halfway down the page when she heard the knock.
Not at the crypt door. Far away. Up through the church, through the passage behind the altar, at Amos's little rotten door into the back lane. Three knocks. Slow. Heavy. Then a pause. Then one more.
Oren was on his feet before the fourth knock had finished. He did it without his crate making a sound, and without his sword making a sound either, though it was in his hand. Lyra had not seen him pick it up.
"That's not Bridie," he said.
"No," said Lyra.
"Bridie knocks like she's trying to break it." He listened. "That's somebody who's knocked on a lot of back doors."
He went. Lyra put the Ledger down on the bench beside Corin and went after him, up the crypt steps, through the cold dark church that smelled of old stone and candle-grease and snow, past the altar with its gray cloth, to the little door. Oren stood to one side of it with his back to the wall and his sword down along his leg and his good hand on the bolt. He looked at her. She nodded.
He opened the door.
An old man stood in the lane with snow on his shoulders.
He was short and broad and very bald, with a round brown face as creased as a walnut, and white eyebrows that stuck out like the eaves of a roof, and a nose that had been broken by a horse a long time ago and set crooked. He wore a long dark blue driving coat with three capes on the shoulders, and the capes were white with snow, and a round hat in his hand. He was holding the hat against his chest with both hands, the way men hold their hats in church.
He looked at Oren. He looked at Oren for a long moment, at his big gray head and his arm in its black sling and the sword along his leg. And then he looked past him, into the dark passage, at Lyra.
And his walnut face did something that Lyra would remember.
It did not smile. It crumpled. All of it. All at once. The way paper crumples in a fist.
"Miss Lyra," said Tibbs.
He had taught her to sit on a horse. Before Oren. Before she could remember. Oren had told her so, on the barge. Old Tibbs put you up on the gray pony when you were three, my lady, and walked round the stable yard with you a hundred times, holding the bridle, and wouldn't let anybody else do it. She did not remember it. She remembered his hands, a little. Big and brown and smelling of saddle soap. Lifting her down.
She had seen him on Friday night. At the bottom of Comb Street, on the box of the Duke's carriage, behind the two gray horses. She had seen him again at Marrow House a week ago, holding a gray mare called Mist in the stable yard. But both times there had been other people. Both times he had only touched his hat and said My lady and looked away.
There was nobody here but Oren.
"Tibbs," she said.
"I've brought you something, miss," said Tibbs. His voice was rough and low and shook a little. "From his Grace."
He let go of the hat with one hand. And reached inside the three-caped coat. And brought out a key.
It was the biggest key Lyra had ever seen. As long as her hand from the wrist to the tip of the middle finger. Black iron, very old, with a great round bow like the handle of a cup, and a long thick shaft, and at the end of the shaft a flat heavy bit cut into teeth like the battlements of a castle. And on the bow, worn nearly smooth by a hundred years of hands, there was a shape. She knew the shape. She had seen it every day of her life until she was eighteen, on the gate, and the door, and the silver, and the seal on her father's desk.
A hand holding a ball.
The Thorne knocker. The one that had been taken off the front door of the house on Crown Walk, and left a pale square behind it.
Tibbs held the key out to her across the step. His big brown hand was shaking.
"The front door," he said. "It's the only one, miss. His Grace has had it on his own watch chain two years. Never let it off him. Not to his steward, not to anybody. He took it off this morning at the seventh bell and gave it to me in the stable yard with his own hand and said, Give this to her, Tibbs, and nobody else. And tell her yes."
Lyra took the key.
It was very cold. And very heavy. Heavier than she had thought anything so small could be. She held it in both hands, in Madame Hesper's thin gray gloves, and looked down at it, at the worn shape on the bow, and did not say anything at all for a long time.
Oren, beside the door, had looked away. He was looking at the wall of the passage, very hard.
"There's a letter too," said Tibbs. "His Grace wrote it himself. And a paper. He said you'd want the paper." He brought them out of the coat. A folded letter, sealed with gold wax, the ship and the key. And a long folded sheet, thicker, cream-colored, with a plum ribbon round it. "And he said I was to say the rest by mouth, because he won't write it down. He said you'd know why."
"Say it," said Lyra.
Tibbs drew himself up a little, in the snow, with his hat against his chest. He said it the way a man says a message he has said over to himself all the way across the city.
"His Grace's second carriage, and his coal wagon, and his own two carts from the home farm, at the bottom of Saint Bride's Lane, at the ninth bell tonight. And Tibbs to drive. And Abner Cole to bring his cart, if he will. Up the Hill by the Mews Road, not the Crescent. In at the back of Crown Walk by the stable gate. Tibbs has the stable key. His Grace will not come himself, because if his Grace is seen on the Mews Road on the Sunday night before Midwinter with four carts, the whole Hill will know it by breakfast. His Grace will be at home, at his own fire, in his own chair, where everybody can see him through the window, all night." Tibbs took a breath. "And he says to tell Lady Lyra Thorne that her mother asked him to keep it shut, and not to let her in. And that he has kept it shut, and he has not let her in. And that her mother never said a word about not letting her daughter in."
Lyra stood very still on the step.
She found that she could not see the old man's face properly. It had gone blurred, at the edges, like the light through the green glass in the tower.
"Tell his Grace," she said. She stopped. She tried again. "Tell his Grace thank you."
"He said you'd say that," said Tibbs. "He said to tell you he doesn't want it. He said to tell you he's been waiting eleven years for somebody to come and ask him for that key, and he'd started to think nobody ever would." He put his hat on. "Ninth bell, miss. The bottom of the lane. I'll be on the box."
He turned to go. And then he turned back.
He looked at Oren.
The two old men looked at each other across the step for a long moment. The short broad bald one in the snow, and the tall gray one in the doorway with his arm in a sling. Twenty-two years they had worked in the same house, Lyra thought. One in the stable yard and one at the foot of the stairs. Twenty-two years of mornings.
"Captain," said Tibbs.
"Tibbs."
"I heard about the shop. On Velvet Street." Tibbs's walnut face worked. "I heard you held the front. On your own."
Oren did not say anything.
"I heard what it cost," said Tibbs.
Oren looked down at the snow.
"Can't read now," he said. "Not a word. Not my own name." He said it quite plainly. The way he said All's well. "I'll know her name, though. The boy drew it me. A boot, and a fork, and a gate with a belly, and a tent."
Tibbs looked at him.
Then he took off his hat again. And held it against his chest. And stood like that in the lane, in the snow, in front of Oren, for a long moment, not saying anything, the way men stand in church when the name of somebody they knew is read out.
Then he put it back on, and nodded, once, and went away down the lane without looking back.
Oren shut the door.
He stood with his good hand flat on it for a while. Then he turned round, and looked at Lyra, at the great black key in her two gloved hands.
"That's the one," he said quietly. "I locked that door every night for twenty-two years, my lady. Last thing. After your father went up." He looked at it. "I know the weight of it."
The Guest List
She read the Duke's letter aloud in the side vault, under the skulls, with everybody who could listen listening.
Corin on his bench, sitting up, with his bad leg out along the stone and his gray hands on the Ledger. Silas in the arch, with his arms folded. Juno on her pallet with her wrapped feet up. Gideon on the floor by the blue chalk shapes. Oren on his crate, with his back to them, as always, and his face to the long hall. He could not read the letter. He would never read anything again. So she read it to him too.
The Duke's hand was big and round and looping, with long tails on the letters that went down into the line below, and blots where the pen had been pressed too hard. It looked like the hand of a man who wrote very few letters and enjoyed every one of them.
My dear Lady Lyra,
Yes.
I find I have nothing to add to that word, and so I shall add a great deal, as old men do.
Tibbs has the key. It has been on my watch chain for two years and I have grown so used to the weight of it that I expect I shall list to the left all day without it. I do not want it back. It is yours. It was always yours. I was only minding it.
You will find the house cold and very dusty and full of sheets. I have had nobody in. Not a maid, not a sweep. Your mother said shut, and I took her at her word, which I find I have done with very few people in my life. The cistern under the yard will be full. The coal in the cellar will be where your father's man left it. There will be mice. Tell the mice I send my regards.
Now. The other matter. Your friend with the leg.
My cellarman is a man called Fenton. He has carried my Marrowmere wine to the Bourse every Midwinter for thirty-one years, in the gold livery, and poured it for me himself, because I will not let the Lady's people touch it. He is a tall, thin, sour man with a gray beard, who walks with a stiff left leg. A Karst musket ball at Highmoor, he says, though I have always believed it was a cart. Everybody at the Bourse knows him. Nobody at the Bourse has looked at his face for thirty years. He is part of the furniture, like the brass box.
Fenton will be taken ill on Monday at noon. Quite ill. I shall send him to his sister's in the country with a basket and a bottle and he will not be back until the spring thaw.
If a tall man with a stiff left leg and Fenton's face should present himself at my back door at the eighth bell on Monday night, in Fenton's livery, to carry my wine, I shall be very glad to see him. And I shall not ask him what he has in his pockets.
I enclose the Lady's list. Every sponsor of an old house is sent one, three days before, so that we may know whom we shall be standing beside, and whom we shall pretend not to know. You will want to read it. I have read it, and I did not enjoy it.
Burn this letter. Keep the list.
Your servant, and your mother's,
Marrow.
When she finished, the vault was quiet for a while.
"The spring thaw," said Silas at last, in a strange voice. "That's three months."
"He's paying the man to be ill for three months," said Juno.
"He's paying him to be ill somewhere else," said Corin. He was looking at his own left leg, stretched out along the bench in its splints. "Somewhere nobody will ask him why he wasn't at the Bourse on Midwinter night." He looked up. "A stiff left leg."
"Yes."
"Thirty-one years, and nobody has looked at his face."
"That's what he says."
Corin did not say anything else. But Lyra saw his mouth go down at the left corner. Just a little.
She put the Duke's letter in the brazier by the arch, the way he had asked, and watched the gold wax melt and the big looping hand go brown and curl and catch. Oren, on his crate, turned his head to watch it burn. He could see that much. He could see a letter burning. He watched until it was gone.
Then she untied the plum ribbon on the list.
It was a single long sheet, folded in three. Thick cream paper, very smooth, the best paper money could buy. At the top, printed in plum-colored ink, in tall thin letters with little curls on them:
THE MEMORY BOURSE.
THE MIDWINTER MASQUERADE.
BY INVITATION OF THE LADY VIVIENNE.
Those who will attend.
And under it, a list. Not printed. Written. In a beautiful clerk's hand, in black ink, with a ruled line under each name. Two columns. Sponsors on the left. Guests on the right.
Lyra read it down slowly, to herself first, and then aloud, the way she read everything now. For Oren.
His Grace the Duke of Marrow. And guest.
The Dowager Lady Ashcombe. And her physician (Dr. Quarles).
Lord and Lady Ost.
The Misses Pellow (three).
Lady Harriet Langley.
The Honourable Fennimore boys. Two. (Not to be given the red.)
Captain Dray, of the Lantern Guard.
And on, and on. Down the left column and on to the right. Half the names she had seen in her aunt's long room on Friday night. Half the names she had grown up hearing on the stairs at Midwinter, through the banisters, in her nightgown, with Rowan beside her. Lords and ladies and councillors and their wives. The Warden of Saint Clement's. Two judges. The master of the Goldsmiths. A man who owned all the ice-houses on the river.
Councillor Thorne. (Councillor C. Thorne.) No guest. No mask.
Lyra stopped there for a moment. Then she went on.
The Treasurer of the Oblivion Bank, Mr. Dorian Sterling. And guest.
The Under-Secretary of the Office of Public Health, Mr. A. Pallister.
From the Ministry of Records, by the Ministry's invitation: the Inquisitor, Mr. S. Kross. And one of his Office.
From the Oblivion Bank, by the Bank's invitation: the Fourth Desk. (One Auditor.)
She stopped again. She did not look at Corin. She knew who the Fourth Desk was. One Auditor. A woman in a dark green coat, in a plain white mask.
And then, at the very bottom of the right-hand column, a little apart from the rest, the way the line about the stones had been apart in Lucian's book, there was one more line. In the same beautiful clerk's hand. With the same ruled line under it.
No name. No sponsor. Just four words.
Guest of the Fourth Desk.
Lyra read it twice.
"What's that?" said Juno from her pallet.
"I don't know."
"Read it again."
"Guest of the Fourth Desk." Lyra looked at it. "That's all. Just that. No name. No mask. It doesn't say who."
"The Auditor's bringing somebody," said Gideon from the floor.
"No," said Corin slowly. He was looking at the list in her hands from across the vault, though he could not have read it from there. "No. Look at the line above. The Fourth Desk. One Auditor. That's her. She doesn't get a guest. The Bank sends one Auditor to watch the box at midnight, under clause eleven. That's all. Auditors don't bring guests." He was quiet a moment. "Guest of the Fourth Desk. Not guest of the Auditor. The Desk. The Desk itself."
"What does that mean?" said Juno.
Nobody answered her.
Lyra looked down at the four words on the cream paper for a long time. Then she folded the list in three again, carefully, along its folds, and tied the plum ribbon round it, and put it in the list pocket in the left side of her mother's gown, where the vial of grayroot had been, and the doctor's letter, and the lily paper. Where Madame Hesper had sewn a pocket for a list.
She noticed one more thing as she put it away. She did not say it out loud. It was not on the list, and so there was nothing to read to Oren.
There was no line for his Excellency.
Not anywhere. Not on the left, not on the right. The man who would come to the Bourse on Monday night at the ninth bell, masked, by the garden door and not the front, and carry his four stones. He was not on the Lady's list at all.
The Lady to be told at the eighth bell, and not before.
Vivienne did not know he was coming.
Lyra pressed her gloved hand flat over the pocket in her mother's gown, over the folded list. And she thought about a room under a glass dome, full of people in masks who all knew exactly whom they would be standing beside, and whom they would pretend not to know. And one man coming in by the garden door whom nobody expected. And how quiet that room would go.
An Old Man Going to Church
He came in by the front door, at the eleventh bell, like an old man going to church on the Sunday before Midwinter. Which was what he was.
Lyra saw him come. She was up in the church itself, in the nave, on her knees by the font, because Silas had sent her up for clean water from the great stone jar that Amos kept filled in the vestry, and the jar was heavy, and she had stopped by the font to rest her arms. The church of Saint Bride's was small and very old and very cold, and nobody used it any more except Amos and the pigeons. There had been no priest for nine years. The pews were black oak, worn smooth, with little doors on the ends that shut. The windows were narrow and high and full of old greenish glass that let in a light like the light at the bottom of a pond. There were saints painted on the walls, very faded, with their faces rubbed away by a hundred years of people touching them for luck. And there was a smell of cold stone and old candle-grease and damp, and under it, faintly, coming up through the floor from the crypt below, the sweet pear smell of the children's breath.
On Sundays a few old women came and sat in the pews for an hour, by themselves, in their shawls, not praying exactly, just sitting. Silas said they had always come, and they always would, priest or no priest. Three of them were there now, in the back pews, with their heads bowed.
The great west door opened with a long groan, and let in a blade of white winter light, and a gust of snow, and an old man.
He stood in the doorway for a moment, getting his breath. A small, bent man, very thin, in a long dark coat buttoned to the chin and a gray wool scarf and a round black hat. He leaned on a stick. A plain stick of dark wood, with a brass ferrule on the end that rang on the stone. He had a parcel under his other arm, a flat square parcel wrapped in oilcloth and tied with string. And round spectacles, with thin gold rims, that had misted over in the warm air of the church, so that for a moment he could not see anything at all and stood there blinking behind two white circles.
Then he took the spectacles off, and wiped them on the end of his scarf, slowly, and put them back on. And Lyra saw his hand.
It was blue.
Not the whole hand. The fingers. To the second knuckle. A deep dark blue, like ink, like the sky after the sun has gone down. As if he had dipped his hands in ink a long time ago, every day for a lifetime, and it had never come out.
She knew who he was. Corin had told her last night. Blue to the second knuckle.
The old man came down the aisle.
He came slowly, tapping with the stick, the brass ferrule ringing on the stone at every step. He did not look at the three old women in the back pews. He did not look at the faded saints. He looked straight ahead of him, at the altar, with its gray cloth, and the little door behind it that went down to the passage and the back lane. As if he knew where it was. As if he had always known.
He stopped by the font.
Lyra had got up off her knees. She stood there in Gideon's thin brown jacket over her mother's gown, with the heavy jar of water at her feet, and looked at him. And he looked at her. Over the top of the gold spectacles, with his head a little on one side, the way birds look at things.
He had a very old face. Older than Tibbs's. Older than anybody's she had ever seen up close. It was thin and fine and folded all over into tiny soft lines, like a letter that has been folded and unfolded a thousand times. His eyes behind the spectacles were pale gray-blue, and watery with the cold, and very bright.
"You'll be the Thorne girl," he said.
His voice was thin and dry and gentle. A voice like paper.
"Yes," said Lyra.
"You have your father's chin." He said it as if he were noting the weather. "And your mother's way of standing. With the weight back on the heels. As if you're ready to take a step back if you need to." He looked at her a moment longer. "I'm Linus Hale. I've come to see Corin Vane. I'm told I'm expected."
"You are," said Lyra.
"Good." He looked down at the stone jar at her feet. "Can I help you with that?"
She almost laughed. He was eighty-one years old, Corin had said, and he could hardly stand.
"No," she said. "Thank you."
"No. Quite right." He nodded. "I'd only drop it."
She picked up the jar. He came behind her, tapping, toward the altar and the little door. And as they passed the end of the front pew, he stopped, and put his blue hand on the black oak of the pew-end, and looked back over his shoulder at the great west door, which had swung shut behind him.
"There's a young man on the wall by the lych gate," he said quietly, "eating a pie. He wrote me down. Old man. Stick. Parcel. Eleventh bell. Went into church." He turned back. "That's quite all right. I am an old man, with a stick and a parcel, and I have gone into church. I wanted him to write it."
"Why?"
Linus Hale looked at her over his spectacles.
"Because when they come to my room, my dear," he said, "they'll read that line in his book. And they'll think, the old fool went to church on the Sunday before Midwinter, to make his peace. And they'll be quite right." He tapped the floor once with his stick. "Lead on."
She led on.
Down through the little door behind the altar, and the passage, and the crypt steps. He went down the steps very slowly, one at a time, with his stick and his hand on the wall, and Oren came up from the crypt to meet him halfway and took his arm without a word. The old man let him. He looked up at Oren's big gray face as they came down together, and said, Thank you, Captain, and Oren said nothing, because he did not like being thanked. But he did not let go of the arm either.
At the bottom of the steps, Linus Hale stopped.
He stood in the arch at the head of the long hall and looked down it. At the low round stone ceiling, and the pillars, and the six braziers burning red in the dim. At the pallets on the floor and in the pews, row after row, with their gray blankets. At the faces on the pallets. At the eyes, open, watching the lamps. At Mrs. Doyle, big and red and cheerful, kneeling by one of them with a cup. At Mrs. Fitch, old and bent, turning a small boy over onto his other side, slowly, the way Silas had shown her.
He breathed in.
Lyra saw him do it. She saw his thin chest go up under the dark coat. And she saw his face change.
"Grayroot," he said.
He said it very softly. Not to her. To nobody. The way you say the name of something you had hoped never to see again.
"Boiled grayroot. Sweet. Like pears going soft in a dish." He shut his eyes behind the gold spectacles. "I have not smelled that in twenty years. Not since the field hospitals at Highmoor, after the last battle in the north. They gave it to the boys who were screaming. To make them quiet. It worked. It always worked. They stopped screaming, and they stopped asking for their mothers, and they stopped knowing their own names, and then they lay very still on their straw and looked at the lamps." He opened his eyes. "And the surgeons called it a kindness. And they wrote it down in the books as eased."
Nobody said anything.
The braziers ticked. Somewhere down the long hall, a child coughed.
Then Linus Hale took his hand off Oren's arm, and tapped his stick once on the floor, and said in his thin dry gentle voice, "Where is he?"
And Lyra took him to the side vault, under the skulls, where Corin was sitting up on his bench with the Ledger on his knee and his gray hands flat on the cover, and his face very white, waiting.
